{{short description|Quasi-Newton root-finding method for the multivariable case}}
In [[numerical analysis]], '''Broyden's method''' is a [[quasi-Newton method]] for [[root-finding algorithm|finding roots]] in {{math|''k''}} variables. It was originally described by [[Charles George Broyden|C. G. Broyden]] in 1965.<ref name="Broyden 1965">{{cite journal |last=Broyden |first=C. G. |author-link=Charles George Broyden |date=1965 |title=A Class of Methods for Solving Nonlinear Simultaneous Equations |journal=Mathematics of Computation |publisher=American Mathematical Society |volume=19 |issue=92 |pages=577–593 |doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-1965-0198670-6 |jstor=2003941 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

[[Newton's method]] for solving {{math|'''f'''('''x''') {{=}} '''0'''}} uses the [[Jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian matrix]], {{math|'''J'''}}, at every iteration. However, computing this Jacobian can be a difficult and expensive operation; for large problems such as those involving solving the [[Kohn–Sham equations]] in [[quantum mechanics]] the number of variables can be in the hundreds of thousands. The idea behind Broyden's method is to compute the whole Jacobian at most only at the first iteration, and to do rank-one updates at other iterations. 

In 1979 Gay proved that when Broyden's method is applied to a linear system of size {{math|''n'' × ''n''}}, it terminates in {{math|2 ''n''}} steps,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Gay |first=D. M. |date=1979 |title=Some convergence properties of Broyden's method |journal=SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis |publisher=SIAM |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=623–630 |doi=10.1137/0716047}}</ref> although like all quasi-Newton methods, it may not converge for nonlinear systems.

== Description of the method ==

=== Solving single-variable nonlinear equation ===

In the [[secant method]], we replace the first derivative {{math|''f''′}} at {{math|''x''<sub>''n''</sub>}} with the [[finite-difference]] approximation:

:<math>f'(x_n) \simeq \frac{f(x_n) - f(x_{n-1})}{x_n - x_{n - 1}},</math>

and proceed similar to [[Newton's method]]:

:<math>x_{n + 1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f^\prime(x_n)}</math>

where {{math|''n''}} is the iteration index.

=== Solving a system of nonlinear equations ===

Consider a system of {{math|''k''}} nonlinear equations in <math>k</math> unknowns
:<math>\mathbf f(\mathbf x) = \mathbf 0 ,</math>

where {{math|'''f'''}} is a [[vector-valued function]] of vector {{math|'''x'''}}

:<math>\mathbf x = (x_1, x_2, x_3, \dotsc, x_k),</math>
:<math>\mathbf f(\mathbf x) = \big(f_1(x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_k), f_2(x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_k), \dotsc, f_k(x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_k)\big).</math>

For such problems, Broyden gives a variation of the one-dimensional Newton's method, replacing the derivative with an approximate [[Jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian]] {{math|'''J'''}}. The approximate Jacobian matrix is determined iteratively based on the '''secant equation''', a finite-difference approximation:

:<math>\mathbf J_n (\mathbf x_n - \mathbf x_{n - 1}) \simeq \mathbf f(\mathbf x_n) - \mathbf f(\mathbf x_{n - 1}),</math>

where {{math|''n''}} is the iteration index. For clarity, define

:<math>\mathbf f_n = \mathbf f(\mathbf x_n),</math>
:<math>\Delta \mathbf x_n = \mathbf x_n - \mathbf x_{n - 1},</math>
:<math>\Delta \mathbf f_n = \mathbf f_n - \mathbf f_{n - 1},</math>

so the above may be rewritten as

:<math>\mathbf J_n \Delta \mathbf x_n \simeq \Delta \mathbf f_n.</math>

The above equation is [[Underdetermined system|underdetermined]] when {{math|''k''}} is greater than one. Broyden suggested using the most recent estimate of the Jacobian matrix, {{math|'''J'''<sub>''n''−1</sub>}}, and then improving upon it by requiring that the new form is a solution to the most recent secant equation, and that there is minimal modification to {{math|'''J'''<sub>''n''−1</sub>}}:

:<math>\mathbf J_n = \mathbf J_{n - 1} + \frac{\Delta \mathbf f_n - \mathbf J_{n - 1} \Delta \mathbf x_n}{\|\Delta \mathbf x_n\|^2} \Delta \mathbf x_n^{\mathrm T}.</math>

This minimizes the [[Matrix norm#Frobenius norm|Frobenius norm]]

:<math>\|\mathbf J_n - \mathbf J_{n - 1}\|_{\rm F} .</math>

One then updates the variables using the approximate Jacobian, what is called a quasi-Newton approach.

:<math>\mathbf x_{n + 1} = \mathbf x_n - \alpha \mathbf J_n^{-1} \mathbf f(\mathbf x_n) .</math>

If <math>\alpha = 1</math> this is the full Newton step; commonly a [[line search ]] or [[trust region]] method is used to control <math>\alpha</math>. The initial Jacobian can be taken as a diagonal, unit matrix, although more common is to scale it based upon the first step.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Shanno |first=D. F. |last2=Phua |first2=Kang -Hoh |date=1978 |title=Matrix conditioning and nonlinear optimization |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01588962 |journal=Mathematical Programming |language=en |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=149–160 |doi=10.1007/BF01588962 |issn=0025-5610|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Broyden also suggested using the [[Sherman–Morrison formula]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sherman |first=Jack |last2=Morrison |first2=Winifred J. |date=1950 |title=Adjustment of an Inverse Matrix Corresponding to a Change in One Element of a Given Matrix |url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.aoms/1177729893 |journal=The Annals of Mathematical Statistics |language=en |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=124–127 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177729893 |issn=0003-4851}}</ref> to directly update the inverse of the approximate Jacobian matrix:

:<math>\mathbf J_n^{-1} = \mathbf J_{n - 1}^{-1} + \frac{\Delta \mathbf x_n - \mathbf J^{-1}_{n - 1} \Delta \mathbf f_n}{\Delta \mathbf x_n^{\mathrm T} \mathbf J^{-1}_{n - 1} \Delta \mathbf f_n} \Delta \mathbf x_n^{\mathrm T} \mathbf J^{-1}_{n - 1}.</math>

This first method is commonly known as the "good Broyden's method."

A similar technique can be derived by using a slightly different modification to {{math|'''J'''<sub>''n''−1</sub>}}. This yields a second method, the so-called "bad Broyden's method":
:<math>\mathbf J_n^{-1} = \mathbf J_{n - 1}^{-1} + \frac{\Delta \mathbf x_n - \mathbf J^{-1}_{n - 1} \Delta \mathbf f_n}{\|\Delta \mathbf f_n\|^2} \Delta \mathbf f_n^{\mathrm T}.</math>

This minimizes a different Frobenius norm

:<math>\|\mathbf J_n^{-1} - \mathbf J_{n - 1}^{-1}\|_{\rm F}.</math>

In his original paper Broyden could not get the bad method to work, but there are cases where it does<ref>{{cite journal |last=Kvaalen |first=Eric |date=1991 |title=A faster Broyden method |journal=BIT Numerical Mathematics |publisher=SIAM |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=369–372 |doi=10.1007/BF01931297}}</ref> for which several explanations have been proposed.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Martı́nez |first=José Mario |date=2000 |title=Practical quasi-Newton methods for solving nonlinear systems |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/s0377-0427(00)00434-9 |journal=Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics |volume=124 |issue=1-2 |pages=97–121 |doi=10.1016/s0377-0427(00)00434-9 |issn=0377-0427|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Marks |first=L. D. |last2=Luke |first2=D. R. |date=2008 |editor-link=Laurence D. Marks |title=Robust mixing for ''ab initio'' quantum mechanical calculations |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1103/physrevb.78.075114 |journal=Physical Review B |volume=78 |issue=7 |doi=10.1103/physrevb.78.075114 |issn=1098-0121|arxiv=0801.3098 }}</ref> Many other quasi-Newton schemes have been suggested in [[Optimization (mathematics)|optimization]] such as the [[BFGS]], where one seeks a maximum or minimum by finding zeros of the first derivatives (zeros of the [[gradient]] in multiple dimensions). The Jacobian of the gradient is called the [[Hessian matrix|Hessian]] and is symmetric, adding further constraints to its approximation.

== The Broyden Class of Methods ==
In addition to the two methods described above, Broyden defined a wider class of related methods.<ref name="Broyden 1965"/>{{rp|578}} In general, methods in the ''Broyden class'' are given in the form<ref name="Nocedal 2006">{{cite book 
|title=Numerical Optimization
|first1=Jorge|last1=Nocedal 
|first2=Stephen J.|last2=Wright
|date= 2006 | publisher=Springer New York 
| series=Springer Series in Operations Research and Financial Engineering 
|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-0-387-40065-5 
| doi=10.1007/978-0-387-40065-5 
| isbn=978-0-387-30303-1}}
</ref>{{rp|150}}  
<math display="block">
\mathbf{J}_{k+1}=\mathbf{J}_k-\frac{\mathbf{J}_k s_k s_k^T \mathbf{J}_k}{s_k^T \mathbf{J}_k s_k}+\frac{y_k y_k^T}{y_k^T s_k}+\phi_k\left(s_k^T \mathbf{J}_k s_k\right) v_k v_k^T,
</math>
where <math>y_k := \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}) - \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_{k}),</math> <math>s_k := \mathbf{x}_{k+1} - \mathbf{x}_k,</math> and <math display="block">v_k = \left[\frac{y_k}{y_k^T s_k} - \frac{\mathbf{J}_k s_k}{s_k^T \mathbf{J}_k s_k}\right],</math>
and <math>\phi_k \in \mathbb{R}</math> for each <math>k = 1, 2, ...</math>.
The choice of <math>\phi_k</math> determines the method.

Other methods in the Broyden class have been introduced by other authors.
* The [[Davidon–Fletcher–Powell formula|Davidon–Fletcher–Powell (DFP) method]], which is the only member of this class being published before the two methods defined by Broyden.<ref name="Broyden 1965"/>{{rp|582}} For the DFP method, <math>\phi_k = 1</math>.<ref name="Nocedal 2006"/>{{rp|150}}
* Anderson's [[iterative method]], which uses a least squares approach to the Jacobian.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Anderson |first=Donald G. |date=1965 |title=Iterative Procedures for Nonlinear Integral Equations |url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/321296.321305 |journal=Journal of the ACM |language=en |volume=12 |issue=4 |pages=547–560 |doi=10.1145/321296.321305 |issn=0004-5411}}</ref>
* Schubert's or sparse Broyden algorithm – a modification for [[sparse matrix|sparse]] Jacobian matrices.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schubert |first=L. K. |date=1970 |title=Modification of a quasi-Newton method for nonlinear equations with a sparse Jacobian |url=https://www.ams.org/mcom/1970-24-109/S0025-5718-1970-0258276-9/ |journal=Mathematics of Computation |volume=24 |issue=109 |pages=27–30 |doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-1970-0258276-9 |issn=0025-5718 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
* The Pulay approach, often used in [[density functional theory]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pulay |first=Péter |date=1980 |title=Convergence acceleration of iterative sequences. the case of scf iteration |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0009261480803964 |journal=Chemical Physics Letters |language=en |volume=73 |issue=2 |pages=393–398 |doi=10.1016/0009-2614(80)80396-4|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kresse |first=G. |last2=Furthmüller |first2=J. |date=1996 |title=Efficient iterative schemes for ab initio total-energy calculations using a plane-wave basis set |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevB.54.11169 |journal=Physical Review B |language=en |volume=54 |issue=16 |pages=11169–11186 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.54.11169 |issn=0163-1829|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* A limited memory method by Srivastava for the root finding problem which only uses a few recent iterations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Srivastava |first=G P |date=1984 |title=Broyden's method for self-consistent field convergence acceleration |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0305-4470/17/6/002 |journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General |volume=17 |issue=6 |pages=L317–L321 |doi=10.1088/0305-4470/17/6/002 |issn=0305-4470|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* Klement (2014) – uses fewer iterations to solve some systems.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Klement |first=Jan |date=2014 |title=On Using Quasi-Newton Algorithms of the Broyden Class for Model-to-Test Correlation |url=http://www.jatm.com.br/ojs/index.php/jatm/article/view/373 |journal=Journal of Aerospace Technology and Management |language=en |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=407–414 |doi=10.5028/jatm.v6i4.373 |issn=2175-9146 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title = Broyden class methods – File Exchange – MATLAB Central|url = http://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/55251-broyden-class-methods|website = www.mathworks.com|access-date = 2016-02-04}}</ref>
* Multisecant methods for [[density functional theory]] problems.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Woods |first=N D |last2=Payne |first2=M C |last3=Hasnip |first3=P J |date=2019 |title=Computing the self-consistent field in Kohn–Sham density functional theory |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-648X/ab31c0 |journal=Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter |volume=31 |issue=45 |pages=453001 |doi=10.1088/1361-648X/ab31c0 |issn=0953-8984|arxiv=1905.02332 }}</ref>
